newsitem.title: USA: Gallaher tobacco spinoff follows lawsuit plans.
newsitem.headline: Gallaher tobacco spinoff follows lawsuit plans.

text.p: American Brands Inc.'s decision Tuesday to spin off its Gallaher tobacco unit and make it liable for smoking lawsuits comes just days after a lawyer said 40 smokers plan to sue the British subsidiary in London.
Just 10 days ago, British lawyer Martyn Day announced that he was coordinating the filing of suits against Gallaher and Imperial Tobacco by the group of smokers who suffer from cancer.

The group action will be the first in Britain in which the plantiffs will be represented by lawyers working on a no-win, no-fee basis. Day said that if the plaintiffs succeed it would open the door to many more suits.
Day said in a telephone interview Tuesday that he plans to file the case by the end of the month.

"The timing of it looks very suspicious in terms of how soon after our announcement it occurred," Day said about American Brands' decision. "Clearly the logic at this stage is the two might be linked. I am therefore wary that there is an attempt to insure the parent company is not affected too badly if we succeed in all these claims against Gallaher."
American Brands spokeman Roger Baker denied that the spinoff was linked to Day's announcement.
"The company spent many months thoroughly reviewing various alternatives so it has nothing to do with anything that happened 10 days ago," he said.

Old Greenwich, Conn.-based American Brands said it would spin off Gallaher to complete its exit from the tobacco business as the U.S. legal and regulatory climate for cigarette companies becomes more threatening.
After the spinoff, American Brands will change its name to Fortune Brands. It said that Gallaher would indemnify Fortune against all tobacco liability.

American Brands sold its U.S. cigarette maker American Tobacco Co. in 1994 to B.A.T Industries Plc, which incorporated the unit into its own Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. Louisville, Ky.-based B&W has assumed all of American Tobacco's liability.

Since 1994, legal attacks on the industry have been mounting steadily with hundreds of individual, class action and state suits filed in the United States over alleged health injuries. In addition, the Food and Drug Administration has won White House approval to regulate cigarettes, an action the industry is challenging.

In London, tobacco companies could face a tough road if the 40 plaintiffs prevail in their expected lawsuit. Under the English legal system one judge is likely to be appointed to deal with the tobacco claims.
Day said that Gallaher's assets would cover the current group of claims, but it was unclear what would happen if there are thousands of future cases.

"The real concern is if we get a judgment in this case it would then affect other cases, we think about 25,000 a year," Day said. "You're talking about sums well in excess of the profits these companies make.
"It (spinoff) would then it would become a very big concern ... if by taking this action the people who were injured cannot get properly paid out."

Richard Daynard, chairman of the Tobacco Products Liability Project, an anti-smoking group located at Boston's Northeastern University, also said he was suspicious about the timing of American Brands' announcement.
He said that while Gallaher would accept tobacco liability under the terms of the spinoff, American Brands' successor Fortune could be liable if Gallaher should go out of business.
"If Gallaher goes belly up, Fortune is still on the hook," he said.
